Everyone waiting for rates to drop is missing what is actually happening in the market right now.

Rates are sitting around 6.6%. Not great. 

But here’s what almost nobody explains to buyers sitting on the sidelines. The market right now favors buyers in a way it has not in years, and that window has a shelf life.

Homebuyer activity just hit a record low. Sellers are sitting on inventory longer. Price cuts are showing up everywhere you look. That combination means the buyers who are still actively shopping have leverage most buyers have not had in a long time.

But... That leverage is temporary. The moment rates drop even half a point, every buyer who has been waiting on the sidelines floods back into the market at the same time. Demand spikes. Sellers stop cutting prices. Multiple offers come back.

The leverage you have today evaporates overnight, and you are back to competing against a crowd for the same house you could negotiate hard on right now.

Meanwhile, rent is not waiting for you to decide. The average renter is paying around $2,000 a month right now nationally. That is $24,000 a year building your landlord’s equity instead of yours. Twelve more months of waiting is $24,000 gone with nothing to show for it, plus whatever the home you want appreciates in the meantime.

So the real choice is not “buy now at a bad rate” versus “wait for a good rate.” It is “negotiate hard while you still have the power” versus “compete against a crowd once you do not.”

You can always refinance a rate later. You cannot refinance a missed negotiation.

Every buyer asks me the same question...

“What’s the interest rate?”

I get why. But it’s not the question that actually matters.

The real question is: Does this monthly payment fit the life you actually want to live?

I’ve watched buyers stretch themselves paper thin just to lock a lower number on paper. I’ve watched them drop thousands on discount points to save $80 a month. I’ve watched them pass on a house they loved because they were waiting on rates to magically drop.

A lower rate does not automatically mean a smarter decision.

Rates today are sitting near 6.6%. That is not going to change because you waited three more months. It might not change this year at all.

Here is what I actually care about when we run your numbers.

Can you still take a vacation without panicking about the payment?
Can you still put money into savings every month?
Can you still say yes to date nights, kids activities, and the small stuff that makes life good?
Can you fall asleep at night without doing mortgage math in your head?

If the answer is yes, that is a good payment. It does not matter what the rate attached to it is.

If rates drop later, great! We talk about refinancing with your lender then. That conversation is easy. But sitting in a house that stretches you thin while you wait on a “perfect” rate that may never show up? That one is hard to undo.

76% of buyers say they would overlook red flags in a home. That number should scare you a little 🫠

I get it. You found the one. The price fits. The location fits. You do not want a home inspection to talk you out of it. 

But here is the stat that should change your mind. More than 7 out of 10 cancelled home purchases fall apart because of what the inspection found, not because the buyer got cold feet.

So before you fall in love, here are the things I make every buyer look at closely, especially on a “starter home” that looks perfect on the surface.

1. Cracks wider than a quarter inch in the foundation, especially horizontal ones or a stair-step pattern in brick. That is not cosmetic. Foundation repairs run anywhere from $10,000 to $50,000 depending on severity.

2. Water stains on ceilings or in the basement, even old ones that look “handled.” Moisture problems come back, and mold remediation is not cheap or fun.

3. Signs of a pest problem. Termites and carpenter ants leave damage that is expensive and sometimes structural.

4. Fresh paint in one weird, specific spot. Nine times out of ten that is not a design choice. That is someone covering something up.

A starter home is supposed to build your equity, not drain it. The whole point is affordability. If you are budgeting $15,000 a year in surprise repairs on a house you bought because it was “cheap,” it was never actually cheap.

Here is my rule for clients: Do not skip the inspection just because you are excited, and do not skip reading the full report just because it is long. The five minutes it takes to actually read it can save you tens of thousands of dollars.

If you are buying soon and want an agent who will slow you down before a $20,000 mistake, comment HIRE and I will send you my free guide on exactly what to look for in an agent who has your back, not just the deal.

Buyers spend twenty minutes staring at the kitchen backsplash and thirty seconds testing the things that actually matter. I flip that ratio every single showing, and it is saved more than one client from buying a house they would have regretted.

Here are the 7 things I make every buyer test before they fall in love with a house.

1. Flush every toilet. Slow refill or a weak flush can mean old plumbing or water pressure problems the whole house shares.

2. Run the shower and the sink at the same time. If the pressure drops, that is your first clue about the pipes you cannot see, and repiping a house is not cheap.

3. Check your cell signal in every room, not just the living room. A dead zone in the primary bedroom is something you live with every single day, and it will not show up on a single listing photo.

4. Open every closet door and cabinet all the way. Sticking doors and hinges that will not close can point to a foundation that has shifted more than the seller wants to admit.

5. Stand in the quietest room and just listen. Traffic, a neighbor’s dog, a nearby train. You are about to sign up for that sound every single night, and a showing on a Tuesday afternoon will not tell you the whole story.

6. Look up, not just around. Water stains, sagging spots, or a ceiling that has been painted in patches. The roof tells the truth even when the seller does not.

7. Check the water heater’s age on the sticker by the tank. If it is past 10 to 12 years old, budget for a replacement instead of being surprised by it six months after closing.

None of these take more than a minute. But together they will tell you more about a house than the staging, the listing photos, and the agent’s pitch ever will.

I can tell within the first five minutes of walking into a house whether the seller actually took care of it. You do not need an inspector for this. You just need to know what to look for.

Here are the 7 things that tell me a house has been neglected, even when the listing photos look perfect.

3. A ceiling corner with slightly different paint than the rest of the room. Someone covered a water stain. I am checking the attic and the roof age before we go any further.

4. Doors that stick, do not latch right, or drag on the floor. That is not just an old house being an old house. That can be foundation movement, and it is not cheap to fix.

5. Weeds growing out of the gutters or a driveway with sealant poured only over the cracks. If they will not maintain what you can see from the street, I promise you they have not been maintaining what you cannot see.

6. A suspiciously new area of caulk or grout in one bathroom while the rest of the grout is filthy and cracked. Selective effort is a red flag, not a good sign.

7. A dryer vent packed with lint, or a furnace filter that looks like it has never been changed. Nobody replaces one system and ignores the rest unless they were only ever doing the bare minimum.

None of these are dealbreakers by themselves. But when I see two or three of them in the same house, I already know what the inspection report is going to say before we even schedule it.

If you’re a seller trying to decide how to sweeten a deal right now, I want you to see the actual math before you default to cutting your price.

Let’s use a real example. A $500,000 home, buyer putting 10% down, financing $450,000 at today’s rate near 6.5%. That buyer’s payment sits around $2,844 a month before taxes and insurance.

Now here are the two moves I see sellers make.

Move one. Cut the price by $20,000. New price is $480,000. Same 10% down, so the loan drops to $432,000. That buyer’s payment falls to about $2,731 a month. Over the life of the loan, they save roughly $22,958 in interest. That’s real money.

It’s just not the biggest number on the table.

Move two. Keep the price exactly where it is and give that same $20,000 as a permanent rate buydown instead. Using standard point pricing, $20,000 on a $450,000 loan buys the rate down to around 5.4%.

That buyer’s payment drops to about $2,524 a month, more than the price cut delivered. And the interest savings over 30 years comes out to roughly $115,394.

Same $20,000. Five times the savings. The buyer feels it every single month in a lower payment, and feels it again decades from now in total interest paid.

Here’s why most sellers still cut price instead. It feels simpler. It feels like something buyers immediately understand. A rate buydown requires a conversation, a lender who can run the numbers, and a seller willing to think past the sticker price on the listing.

But if your goal is getting your home under contract with a buyer who feels like they got a real win, the buydown does more with the same dollar. It solves the payment problem buyers are actually stuck on in this rate environment, not just the number on the sign.

Before you agree to your next price reduction, ask your agent to run both numbers side by side. The difference might change your entire strategy.

Everyone wants to know if it is a buyer’s market or a seller’s market right now.

And it’s not really either. 

The 2026 market is something most people do not have a clean word for. Home sales are at a 5-month high. But buyer demand is fragile. Inventory is up in most markets. But the inventory that is actually affordable is not. Rates are at 6.4% and easing slightly. But affordability is still stretched by any historical measure.

This is not a buyer’s market or a seller’s market. It is a hyperlocal market. Meaning what is happening on your block is often completely different from what is happening three zip codes away.

Here is what I tell every seller trying to navigate this.

1. Stop reading national headlines as if they apply to your listing. The national numbers are an average of thousands of very different micro-markets. Your neighborhood has its own supply, its own demand, and its own buyer pool.

2. Price like a surgeon, not a gambler. In a market like this, overpricing by even 3% can mean sitting for 60 days while an otherwise identical home priced correctly sells in two weeks.

3. The first offer is usually the best one. I know sellers who passed on strong first offers waiting for something better in a market that was not going to deliver it. Be ready to move on the right offer when it shows up.

4. Know your buyer’s likely situation. Right now, the buyer most likely to close is either a first-time buyer using assistance programs or a move-up buyer with significant equity from a previous sale. Understanding which one you are marketing to changes how you price, stage, and negotiate.

5. Negotiate on structure, not just price. A clean offer at asking with flexible timing can be worth more than a higher offer with a complicated contingency stack.

The sellers winning right now are not guessing. They are working with someone who understands the specific dynamics of their market.

I have been watching something closely in this market. 

Deals are falling apart more than they have in years. And most buyers have no idea why until it happens to them.

Pending listings rose 4.3 percent year over year in May. Buyers are out there and active. But the gap between going under contract and actually closing has gotten a lot messier.
Here is what is driving it.

First, buyers have more leverage than they have had since before 2020. More inventory means more options. And buyers with options negotiate. They make inspection requests. They push back on appraisal gaps. They ask for credits. When sellers refuse to budge, deals die.

Second, real estate fraud is accelerating. AI is being used to clone email communication, forge closing documents, and impersonate title companies. Deals fall apart when wire fraud is discovered at the worst possible moment. And buyers who are not working with experienced agents are the ones most exposed.

Third, a lot of buyers are stretching thin to get into a home at current rates and prices.

When an inspection reveals deferred maintenance or a repair list, they panic. They back out because they have no financial cushion left to absorb surprises.

Here is how I help my buyers stay in contract when things get hard.

1. Get a thorough pre-inspection mindset from day one. Know what you can tolerate before you fall in love with a house.

2. Build a small reserve into your budget for closing surprises. Even $5,000 set aside changes how you respond to an inspection report.

3. Verify every wire instruction by phone with a known number. Not the one from the email. Every single time.

You do not want one buyer considering your home, you want a line. Traffic creates urgency. Urgency creates leverage. Leverage is what actually protects your price at the negotiating table.
